description: We are 3 high school students from Ankara/Turkiye. Our ultimate goal as orbitrangers is to build a project that can have an impact worldwide and expand many horizons. We are willing to put great effort into our project.
summary:
Orbit+ is a self-regulating health monitoring system designed for astronauts operating in outer space. In long expeditions, including Mars, delays in communication with the Earth could be up to several minutes, therefore, astronauts should regulate their health independently. Orbit+ integrates information collected from smart suit sensors, cabin environment, questionnaires, crew activities schedule, resources, and equipment condition into one dashboard according to NASA's five hazards of space flight: radiation, isolation, distance from the Earth, gravity fields, and closed environment.

As opposed to other systems which operate on average values, Orbit+ learns personalized baseline of each astronaut online through z-score calculations and provides individual recommendations about sleeping, stress, and mood management. If the connection is cut, it holds notifications and uploads them when the connection gets restored. It is a functional prototype that uses synthetic data and assists decision-making.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Orbit+ is an autonomous health-monitoring platform for astronauts on deep-space missions. On a Mars-class mission, a message to Earth and back can take up to 20 minutes, so a crew cannot wait for ground control to interpret a health problem. Orbit+ runs locally and brings scattered data into one dashboard organized around NASA’s five spaceflight hazards: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile/closed environments.

It combines four data sources:

  • Smart-suit sensors: heart rate, HRV, respiration, SpO₂, body temperature, blood pressure, sweat (EDA), cortisol, muscle fatigue and balance.
  • Cabin environment: radiation dose rate, CO₂, pressure, temperature, humidity and noise.
  • Daily survey and schedule: sleep, mood, stress, exercise, nutrition, water, pain, dizziness and vision. Uploading the daily schedule (EVA, exercise, meetings, shifts) automatically adds relevant survey questions.
  • Resources and equipment: food, water and oxygen stock versus mission length, equipment failures and the ground-link status.

Each astronaut gets a personal baseline model that learns online from their own measurements. For every sensor it tracks a running mean and variance (EWMA) and scores each new reading with a z-score. Readings three or more standard deviations away are not learned, so an illness or fault is never mistaken for the “new normal”. The model is stored on the device, so early data is never forgotten. The system also separates a sudden radiation spike (suspected solar event) from steady background radiation, and combines risks (for example, sleep deficit plus workload amplifies stress). When the link to Earth is down, alerts are queued and forwarded to ground control once contact returns.

What benefits does it have?

  • Faster, local decisions without waiting for ground control.
  • Early warnings that are personal rather than based on population averages.
  • Every alert explains itself: which parameter, how far from the person’s baseline, and what to do.
  • One screen for the crew and a flight-surgeon report for medical review.
  • Personalized sleep, stress and morale guidance based on each person’s data, schedule and location on the station.

What is the intended impact?

The goal is to reduce health risk and mission dependence on Earth as missions get longer and farther. The same approach applies wherever help is far away: Antarctic stations, submarines, offshore platforms and remote expeditions. Orbit+ is a decision-support tool; it supports the crew and flight surgeon and does not diagnose.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages and frameworks: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React 18 and Tailwind CSS.
  • Visualization: SVG body map and live sparkline charts.
  • Storage: browser localStorage, with no server or cloud, so data stays on the device.
  • Offline use: designed to run offline in the browser after the first load.
  • Knowledge base: NASA Human Research Program risk pages and the NASA Space Apps challenge resources.
  • Hardware: none required. The smart suit and cabin sensors are simulated, and the data model mirrors what real wearable sensors would provide, so real data can replace the simulator.

How is it creative?

  • It treats astronaut health as one connected system instead of separate parameters.
  • It learns each person’s own baseline and measures deviation statistically, instead of using fixed thresholds alone.
  • Its survey adapts to the daily schedule.
  • It models the communication delay itself as a health hazard, with queued alerts and autonomous protocols.
  • It includes habitat and morale support: room-by-room oxygen, noise, temperature and lighting suggestions, and crew-location awareness.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Communication delay: the system must work without Earth.
  • Explainability: a medical-style tool must justify every alert, which is why we chose transparent statistics over a black-box model.
  • Limited data: with no real astronaut data available, online statistical learning works from small data and can later be replaced by time-series models.
  • Usability under stress: a clear, color-coded interface that is readable at a glance.
  • Privacy: health data stays on the device.
  • Safety and honesty: thresholds and sensor data are demo simulations, and the interface states that it is not a medical diagnosis.
  • Crew diversity: roles, individual baselines and per-person recommendations.
  • Next steps: validating thresholds with a flight surgeon and published NASA data, adding real sensor input, and moving to encrypted storage with ground-control sync.
